strengths: The paper addresses an important problem in conditional image generation: improving underrepresented classes without sacrificing head-class quality. The combination of unconditional feature repulsion and timestep-weighted conditional–unconditional alignment is simple and applicable to both U-Net and transformer architectures.

Experiments cover five datasets and multiple sampling settings. Improvements are substantial on the larger benchmarks: ImageNet-LT FID decreases from 19.95 to 16.41 at 160 epochs, while TinyImageNet-LT tail FID decreases from 40.12 to 30.39. Places-LT also improves across head, body, and tail groups.

The ablations provide useful evidence that both losses contribute. Without resampling, combining them improves TinyImageNet-LT FID from 18.67 to 17.16. Table 5 additionally demonstrates that CCUA improves recall when combined with resampling, whereas resampling alone decreases recall.

The manuscript appropriately acknowledges closely related dispersive regularization and GAN-based conditional–unconditional sharing. It also reports training overhead, unchanged inference latency, and a small three-seed robustness study on CIFAR100-LT.
weaknesses: The strongest comparisons do not fully isolate the proposed contribution from resampling. Table 5 shows that resampling alone accounts for much of the 40-epoch ImageNet-LT FID improvement: 33.87 to 28.05, versus 25.89 for the complete method. The corresponding resampling-controlled comparisons against SiT and Dispersive Loss are missing at later checkpoints. DiffROP is discussed as a particularly relevant predecessor but is not evaluated. These omissions leave the advantage over closely related alternatives insufficiently established.

The contrastive objective is underspecified in a technically consequential way. Equation 1 uses unnormalized dot products, but Section 3.1 assumes constant self-similarity and embeddings on a hypersphere. Without explicit normalization, increasing feature norms can reduce the objective without producing the claimed angular dispersion, and log N need not be its maximum. Normalization and feature aggregation must be specified to assess both implementation and reasoning.

Important reproducibility details are absent: values of the loss weights alpha and gamma, the precise resampling rule, and the SiT configuration and adaptation of the DDPM noise-alignment objective to its interpolant parameterization. Appendix A.1 provides useful training budgets but does not resolve these choices. The evaluation reference split, generated class distribution, and guidance-search selection protocol also need clarification.

Evidence for the central tail-diversity claim remains incomplete. ImageNet-LT reports aggregate precision and recall without head/tail breakdowns, while pooled tail FID on the other datasets does not directly measure within-class coverage or conditional correctness. Selected samples and t-SNE visualizations are suggestive but cannot establish distributional coverage or reduced memorization across classes.

The alignment mechanism is plausible but not adequately isolated. There is no comparison of constant versus timestep-weighted alignment, or conditional versus unconditional placement of the same contrastive loss. Moreover, Equation 6 replaces the timestep-dependent factor from the Gaussian KL derivation with t/T, making it a reweighted surrogate rather than the stated KL objective. The paper should distinguish this heuristic from the derivation and test the design choices supporting its novelty.

Some claims exceed the reported evidence. Section 4.2 claims improvements across all head/body/tail groups, but TinyImageNet-LT head FID is 21.32 versus 21.27 for DDPM and 20.64 for OCLT. Balanced-data DDPM is also incorrectly described as a theoretical optimum. These are correctable presentation issues; the more substantive reasons for a borderline rejection are the incomplete controlled comparisons and method specification.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant computer-vision problem: improving conditional generation for underrepresented classes. The combination of unconditional feature repulsion and timestep-weighted conditional–unconditional alignment is simple and applicable to both U-Net and transformer architectures.

The empirical results are promising across five datasets. At 160 epochs, ImageNet-LT FID improves from 19.95 to 16.41 and recall from 18.61% to 21.34%. Tail-group FID improves from 40.12 to 30.39 on TinyImageNet-LT and from 23.74 to 20.84 on Places-LT.

The experiments include useful component and resampling ablations, several sampling budgets, and a three-seed CIFAR100-LT comparison. Table 5 demonstrates a benefit beyond resampling alone: FID improves from 28.05 to 25.89 while recall increases from 17.26% to 23.05%.
Related methods are explicitly acknowledged, including UTLO, DiffROP, and dispersive regularization. The appendix candidly reports increased training cost and unchanged inference latency.
weaknesses: Essential implementation details are missing. Neither the main text nor appendix specifies the loss coefficients α and γ, feature normalization or aggregation for Eq. 1, or the precise adaptation of the DDPM noise-alignment objective to SiT. These omissions materially hinder reproduction of the central contribution.

The mathematical explanation of UCL assumes properties absent from its definition. With the unnormalized dot products written in Eq. 1, self-similarity is not constant, collapse need not maximize the loss, and increasing feature norms can reduce the objective without improving angular diversity. Explicit unit normalization would resolve much of this issue, but even then feature dispersion does not establish diversity of generated images.

The central claim concerns within-class tail diversity, but ImageNet-LT reports only aggregate metrics, and the smaller datasets primarily report pooled tail-group FID. These measurements do not directly establish within-class coverage or preservation of label fidelity under alignment. Selected images and t-SNE density plots provide suggestive evidence, but class-conditioned coverage, label accuracy, and quantitative memorization measurements would substantially strengthen the case.

The novelty is mainly the combination and placement of mechanisms closely related to acknowledged prior work. The experiments do not sufficiently isolate the claimed advantage of unconditional-space regularization: there is no matched conditional-versus-unconditional UCL comparison, no alignment-weighting ablation, and no empirical comparison with DiffROP. Table 5 usefully controls resampling at 40 epochs, but corresponding controls for the principal 160-epoch result and the dispersive-loss baseline are missing.

The KL derivation justifies a timestep-dependent multiple of noise-prediction MSE; replacing that coefficient with t/T is a heuristic, rather than the same KL objective. The paper should distinguish these statements and experimentally support the chosen weighting. Similar early trajectories from a shared noise initialization also do not by themselves demonstrate beneficial head-to-tail knowledge transfer.

Some claims overstate the evidence. Section 4.2 claims the best FID across every group, although TinyImageNet-LT head FID is 21.32 versus 20.64 for OCLT and 21.27 for DDPM. A model trained on balanced data is also not a theoretical performance bound. These are correctable presentation issues; the more consequential concerns are reproducibility and evidence for the proposed mechanism. Overall, the substantial reported gains make this a close decision, but those unresolved concerns slightly favor rejection under Algorithms/General.

strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful computer-vision problem: improving diversity and fidelity for underrepresented classes in conditional image generation. Assessed as Algorithms/General, its contribution is a practical combination of unconditional feature repulsion and timestep-weighted conditional–unconditional alignment.

The empirical gains are consistent across five datasets and both U-Net and transformer architectures. On ImageNet-LT at 160 epochs, CCUA improves FID from 19.95 to 16.41 and recall from 18.61% to 21.34%, with only a small precision decrease. Comparisons include relevant long-tailed methods and the closely related Dispersive Loss.

The strongest direct evidence for the central claim comes from the category-specific results: tail FID improves from 40.12 to 30.39 on TinyImageNet-LT and from 23.74 to 20.84 on Places-LT. Qualitative examples and nearest-neighbor visualizations provide additional, albeit illustrative, evidence of reduced repetition.

The ablations support contributions from both losses. Without resampling, combining them improves TinyImageNet-LT FID from 18.67 to 17.16. Table 5 also shows that CCUA improves recall when combined with resampling, whereas resampling alone reduces recall.

The approach adds no inference latency and acknowledges its additional training cost. The appendix provides useful sampling-step comparisons, a small multi-seed experiment, and implementation details. Related conditional–unconditional GAN methods and representation regularizers are explicitly credited.
weaknesses: Important reproduction details are missing. The manuscript does not specify the loss weights α and γ, feature normalization or pooling for UCL, or precisely how the noise-prediction alignment is implemented in the SiT flow formulation. Normalization is especially consequential: Eq. (1) uses raw dot products, whereas the explanation assumes constant self-similarity and a hypersphere. Without normalization, increasing feature norms can reduce the loss without the claimed angular dispersion.

The strongest ImageNet-LT comparisons partly conflate the proposed losses with resampling. At 40 epochs, resampling alone improves FID from 33.87 to 28.05, compared with 25.89 for the full method. This ablation is informative, but resampling-matched SiT and Dispersive Loss comparisons are absent at the longer training budgets. The reported 1.48× SiT and 1.6× DDPM training overhead also warrants a matched-compute comparison.

Evidence for tail-specific diversity is incomplete at the flagship ImageNet-LT scale: Table 1 reports aggregate precision and recall, without head/tail breakdowns or class-consistency measurements. Pooled tail FID on smaller datasets cannot by itself establish improved within-class coverage. Class-conditional precision/recall and quantitative memorization measurements would better distinguish useful diversity from semantic drift.

The proposed mechanism is plausible but insufficiently isolated. There is no comparison of unconditional versus conditional feature regularization under otherwise identical settings, nor an ablation of the alignment timestep weighting. UCL acts on noisy training-image features, so improved generated-image diversity is an empirical outcome rather than a direct mathematical consequence. Similarly, Eq. (6) replaces the timestep-dependent scaling of the Gaussian KL with a heuristic linear weight.

Some statements overreach the evidence. Section 4.2 claims improvement across every category, but TinyImageNet-LT head FID is 21.32 versus 21.27 for DDPM and 20.64 for OCLT. Balanced-data DDPM is also described as a theoretical optimum despite being only an empirical reference. These are correctable presentation issues; more substantively, the evaluation should specify the real reference split, generated class distribution, and guidance-selection protocol more clearly.

strengths: The paper addresses an important computer-vision problem: improving class-conditional generation when tail classes have very little training data. As an Algorithms/General contribution, combining unconditional feature dispersion with timestep-weighted conditional–unconditional alignment is a plausible, straightforward approach.

The empirical improvements are substantial and span U-Net and transformer architectures across five datasets. At 900k ImageNet-LT training steps, Table 1 reports FID improving from 19.9 to 15.1 and tail FID from 33.9 to 22.5. Tables 2–3 also show improved tail performance on TinyImageNet-LT and Places-LT without degrading head FID relative to DDPM.

The experiments include relevant competing methods, individual-loss ablations, resampling controls, feature-layer choices, timestep schedules, and an extreme imbalance setting. Resampling-controlled results still support an incremental benefit from CCUA: ImageNet-LT FID improves from 16.7 to 15.1 at 900k steps.

The method is clearly illustrated, and related work on unconditional knowledge sharing and dispersive regularization is explicitly acknowledged. The appendix reports training overhead and an optimized implementation; the comparison between 700k CCUA steps and 900k SiT steps provides useful evidence that improvements are not solely due to additional computation.
weaknesses: The theoretical justification in Section 3.2 does not establish the claimed superiority of unconditional contrastive learning. Equation 1 contrasts a normalized representation with itself, so the standard InfoNCE argument does not directly establish the asserted bound on mutual information between the representation and the clean image. Increasing a lower bound also does not necessarily increase the underlying mutual information. Moreover, unconditional features can still encode class identity or distinguish injected noise, especially at large timesteps. The chain-rule decomposition therefore does not prove that removing explicit conditioning eliminates shortcuts or improves within-class semantic diversity.

The proposed transfer of diversity from unconditional to conditional hidden features is not established by the alignment objective. Equations 3–8 align output noise predictions, rather than the hidden representations regularized by UCL. Matching outputs through a non-injective decoder need not align hidden features or transfer their diversity. The Gaussian calculation motivates output matching under its assumptions, but it does not demonstrate the stronger latent-distillation mechanism claimed throughout the paper.

Evidence for the central diversity claim is mixed. At 900k steps, the main ImageNet-LT model improves precision but reduces recall from 18.6% to 17.3%; Table 6 likewise shows no recall improvement under extreme imbalance. Table 13 demonstrates a potentially useful fidelity–recall tradeoff with the final-layer variant, but lower pooled tail FID alone does not establish greater within-class diversity. Tail-specific coverage, conditional accuracy, and quantitative memorization measurements would be more convincing than selected examples and t-SNE density plots.

Resampling accounts for a substantial fraction of the headline improvements, complicating attribution and comparisons with prior regularizers. In Table 12, resampling alone reduces ImageNet-LT FID from 19.9 to 16.7, versus 15.1 with CCUA. The appendix acknowledges and partially controls this, but the main comparisons do not clearly establish equivalent resampling and tuning for competing methods. A matched comparison of conditional versus unconditional dispersion, each with the same alignment loss, resampling, feature layer, and tuning budget, is particularly important to support the claimed advantage over Dispersive Loss.

Reproducibility and uncertainty reporting remain incomplete. The manuscript does not clearly specify the SiT model size, exact resampling distribution, feature pooling or flattening operation, or the translation of the DDPM noise-alignment objective to SiT training. Evaluation reference splits, class-sampling proportions, and guidance-search details are insufficiently documented; tail definitions also differ between Section 4.2 and Appendix A.1. No repeated-run uncertainty is provided, which matters for smaller component gains. Overall, the practical results are promising, but the mechanism and controlled evidence leave a slight preference for rejection.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem in class-conditional generation: improving underrepresented classes without sacrificing head-class quality. As an Algorithms/General submission, its principal contribution is a simple combination of unconditional feature repulsion and timestep-weighted conditional–unconditional output alignment.

The empirical improvements are substantial and extend across architectures and datasets. On ImageNet-LT at 900k steps, Table 1 reports FID improving from 19.9 to 15.1 and tail FID from 33.9 to 22.5. Tables 2–3 show improvements on TinyImageNet-LT and Places-LT, with head-class FID maintained or improved relative to DDPM.

The experimental coverage is extensive: multiple training durations, loss-component and feature-layer ablations, resampling controls, extreme imbalance, and additional sampling configurations. Comparisons include relevant long-tailed methods, REPA, and dispersive regularization.

The method is practically straightforward and does not require an external representation teacher. Appendix A.2 quantifies training overhead and provides an implementation optimization. The paper also appropriately acknowledges its relationship to prior conditional–unconditional GAN methods and dispersive regularization.
weaknesses: The theoretical argument distinguishing unconditional from conditional contrastive learning is not established. Section 3.2 invokes the standard InfoNCE mutual-information interpretation without deriving its applicability to the self-positive objective in Eq. 1 or distinguishing clean-image information from injected noise. Maximizing I(h;c) does not establish that within-class collapse optimizes the full contrastive objective, which also repels same-class examples. Unconditional representations can likewise encode class identity or noise. Consequently, the claim of theoretical superiority is stronger than the analysis supports.

The proposed mechanism also conflates output alignment with latent alignment. Equation 8 matches predicted noise, whereas the repulsion operates on intermediate features. Matching outputs through a non-injective decoder does not guarantee that conditional features inherit unconditional feature diversity. This does not invalidate the empirical method, but the central explanation needs direct evidence or more cautious wording.

Evidence for improved diversity is mixed. At 900k steps, the main ImageNet-LT configuration improves precision but decreases recall from 18.6% to 17.3% (Table 1); under extreme imbalance, recall is lower or unchanged (Table 6). Other feature-layer choices improve recall (Table 13), so the issue is a quality–coverage tradeoff rather than uniformly unsuccessful diversification. However, pooled tail FID and selected visualizations do not establish increased within-class coverage. Tail-specific recall, class-consistency measurements, and broader memorization analysis would better substantiate the principal claim.

Resampling accounts for a substantial fraction of the headline gains. In Table 12, resampling alone improves ImageNet-LT FID from 19.9 to 16.7, versus 15.1 for the complete method. The controls demonstrate an additional benefit from CCUA, but corresponding resampling-matched results for Dispersive Loss and other competitors are not provided. A controlled comparison of conditional versus unconditional repulsion with identical resampling, feature layer, weighting, and alignment is particularly important to establish the distinctive contribution.

Reproducibility and uncertainty reporting remain incomplete. Appendix A.1 omits several consequential details, including the precise resampling distribution and the reference-set and class-sampling protocol for FID evaluation. No repeated-run variability is reported, making smaller loss-component gains difficult to assess. Overall, the promising empirical results make this a close decision, but the unresolved attribution and diversity-evidence concerns support a slight preference for rejection.

strengths: As an Algorithms/General submission, the paper addresses an important problem: improving class-conditional diffusion generation when tail classes have very few examples. Combining unconditional feature repulsion with timestep-weighted conditional–unconditional alignment is a useful, straightforward adaptation applicable to both U-Net and transformer architectures.

The quality improvements are substantial and reasonably broad. On ImageNet-LT at 900k steps, CCUA improves FID from 19.9 to 15.1 and tail FID from 33.9 to 22.5, outperforming the reported CBDM, REPA, and Dispersive Loss baselines. Improvements also extend to TinyImageNet-LT, Places-LT, and CIFAR variants. Table 3 supports preservation of head-class quality on the two evaluated datasets.

The experimental analysis includes individual-loss ablations, resampling controls, feature-layer choices, alignment schedules, multiple sampling budgets, and a more extreme imbalance setting. Crucially, gains remain beyond resampling alone: ImageNet-LT FID improves from 16.7 to 15.1 at 900k steps, and TinyImageNet-LT tail FID improves from 33.6 to 30.4.

The paper acknowledges computational overhead and reports an approximately matched-training-time comparison: CCUA at 700k steps outperforms vanilla SiT at 900k steps. Qualitative examples and nearest-neighbor visualizations provide additional, although limited, support for improved generation. These empirical merits support a slight preference for acceptance.
weaknesses: The central claim of improved intra-class diversity is less established than the quality gains. In Table 1, the final CCUA model improves precision but decreases overall recall from 18.6% to 17.3%; Table 6 similarly shows no consistent recall improvement. This does not disprove tail-specific gains, but pooled tail FID cannot isolate intra-class coverage or class correctness. Tail-specific recall, class-consistency measurements, and aggregate memorization analysis would strengthen the claim beyond selected examples and t-SNE visualizations.

The theoretical justification in Section 3.2 overreaches. The standard InfoNCE mutual-information interpretation is not established for the particular self-positive objective and the claimed information about clean images. Moreover, unconditional representations can still encode class information, noise, or timestep, so removing explicit conditioning does not eliminate shortcuts or guarantee semantic diversity. Likewise, aligning output noise predictions does not guarantee alignment of intermediate features through a non-injective decoder. The claimed theoretical superiority should be qualified as a hypothesis.

Resampling accounts for much of the headline improvement: at 250k ImageNet-LT steps, it reduces FID from 33.8 to 28.1, compared with 27.0 for the main CCUA configuration. Although the resampling ablations are valuable, equally explicit resampling-matched comparisons against Dispersive Loss and other competitors are needed to isolate the proposed mechanism. The compute-matched comparison also uses vanilla SiT rather than the stronger resampled baseline.

Reproducibility remains incomplete. The appendix does not fully specify the SiT model configuration, the mathematical resampling rule, feature aggregation for contrastive similarity, or how the DDPM-derived alignment objective is implemented for SiT's prediction parameterization and time convention. It also introduces timestep weighting for UCL that is absent from Equation 1 and Algorithm 1. Evaluation reference splits and generated class proportions need clearer specification.

No repeated-run uncertainty is reported, limiting confidence in smaller component-level gains. Originality also lies primarily in the combination and adaptation: unconditional knowledge sharing is motivated by prior GAN work, and negative-only repulsion closely resembles Dispersive Loss. Claims that both losses are independently novel and that balanced-data DDPM results constitute a theoretical performance bound should be moderated.
